title: Conversions with powers, rates, and offsets
objective: Convert signed quantities, areas, volumes, inverse units, and compound rates with explicit unit cancellation, and distinguish temperature values from temperature differences.
why: Areas, rates, densities, and temperature changes occur throughout physics and circuit measurements. Writing cancellation explicitly prevents a familiar linear conversion from being applied incorrectly to a square, cube, denominator, or offset scale.

prerequisites.label: SI quantities, prefixes, and engineering notation

sections.heading: Quick recall
paragraphs: A conversion factor is a ratio equal to one, arranged to cancel the old unit. Raise the whole factor to the unit's power. Convert numerator and denominator separately in a rate.

Absolute Celsius and kelvin values satisfy $T/\mathrm K=t/{}^\circ\mathrm C+273.15$. Temperature differences have equal numerical values in kelvins and Celsius degrees: an offset cancels on subtraction. Read the worked examples, then use the checkpoint to check this distinction independently.

sections.heading: Cancellation explains the direction
paragraphs: The equality 1 s=1000 ms gives both 1 s/(1000 ms) and 1000 ms/(1 s), each equal to one. Multiply by the one whose denominator cancels the source unit. A signed interval or coordinate remains signed because the conversion factor is positive.

Do not replace units only after finishing numerical arithmetic. Carry them through multiplication and division. If the intended target is m/s but your expression leaves ms²/m, the algebra of the units has already identified a setup error.

sections.heading: A square unit contains two length factors
paragraphs: An area of 1 cm² means (1 cm)(1 cm), not one hundredth of a square metre. Both length factors convert, so $1\,\mathrm{cm^2}=10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^2}$. A cubic unit contains three length factors and an inverse unit reverses the exponent.

The same rule applies to a prefixed unit in parentheses: $(10^{-3}\,\mathrm m)^3=10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m^3}$. For inverse centimetres, $(10^{-2}\,\mathrm m)^{-1}=10^2\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$. Writing parentheses around the whole conversion protects the exponent.

sections.heading: A rate combines independent conversions
paragraphs: For a speed, convert distance and elapsed time. Since 1 km=1000 m and 1 h=3600 s, multiplying km/h by 1000/3600 gives m/s. The inverse conversion multiplies by 3.6. That factor is not a new physical law; it comes from unit equalities.

Two prefixes can cancel numerically while the units still require care. One mV per ms equals one V per s because both numerator and denominator scale by 10^-3. In density, one gram per cubic centimetre becomes 1000 kilograms per cubic metre: the mass factor is 10^-3 but the volume factor is 10^-6.

sections.heading: An offset scale needs addition as well as scaling
paragraphs: The Celsius and kelvin scales have equal-size increments but different zero locations. A Celsius temperature of 25 corresponds to 298.15 K. A rise of 25 Celsius degrees corresponds to a rise of 25 K; adding 273.15 to a difference would count the offset incorrectly.

For two readings, $(t_2+273.15)-(t_1+273.15)=t_2-t_1$. State whether your number is a value on a temperature scale or a change. This refresher uses ordinary thermodynamic temperatures and excludes values below zero kelvin; it does not teach thermodynamics or sensor calibration.

examples.title: Convert an area

steps.reason: Square the complete ratio because the old unit occurs twice.

examples.conclusion: The area is 0.00025 m², not 0.025 m².

examples.title: Convert a volume

steps.reason: Apply the cube to both the factor and metre unit.
Multiply the original number by the cubic conversion.

examples.conclusion: A small length conversion becomes much smaller when cubed.

examples.title: Convert a density

steps.reason: Mass and volume have different conversion exponents.
Subtract the denominator exponent when dividing.

examples.conclusion: The density is 1200 kg/m³; the exact conversion does not add precision.

examples.title: Distinguish a temperature from a change
examples.prompt: Convert 25 °C and a rise of 25 °C to kelvins.

steps.reason: The temperature value needs the zero-location offset.
Subtracting two values cancels the same offset.

examples.conclusion: The temperature is 298.15 K; the change is 25 K.

guided.title: Finish the reasoning
guided.setup: A surface has area 3 cm². A voltage rises by 6 mV over 2 ms. Set up each conversion before simplifying.
before: Area needs two factors of the length conversion.
The voltage rate has a numerator conversion and a denominator conversion.

question.prompt: Convert 3 cm² to m² and calculate the rate for a +6 mV change in 2 ms in V/s.
hints: Write the supplied quantities and their units first.
The voltage rate has a numerator conversion and a denominator conversion.
Three square centimetres is 3*(0.01 m)^2=0.0003 m².
explanation: Three square centimetres is 3*(0.01 m)^2=0.0003 m².
The rate is 0.006 V / 0.002 s=3 V/s; the milli factors cancel.
question.answerSummary: Three square centimetres is 3*(0.01 m)^2=0.0003 m². The rate is 0.006 V / 0.002 s=3 V/s; the milli factors cancel.

guided.after: Explain each conversion before starting independent practice. Guided feedback is assisted work, not checkpoint evidence.

interaction.prompt: Change a length-unit power among 1,2,3,-1 and predict the full scale factor. Show factor cancellation and a labeled table; compare area conversion with conversion of a side length.

summary: Use ratios equal to one and cancel the old units visibly.
Apply powers to entire conversion factors; convert rate numerators and denominators separately.
An absolute temperature uses an offset; a temperature difference does not.
retrieval: Convert 5 cm^-1 to m^-1 without a calculator. Then explain why a cooling of 8 °C is a change of -8 K rather than 265.15 K.
